answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.1:2021, Clause 4.6.3.2(d) requires that a reduced pressure zone device (RPZD) "have the relief drain outlet located not less than 300 mm above the finished surface level". So the minimum height is 300 mm above the finished surface level. The same clause also requires free ventilation to the atmosphere for the relief valve outlet at all times, and that the device not be located in an area that may be subjected to ponding or freezing. Note that the parallel provision for a reduced pressure detector assembly (RPDA), Clause 4.6.3.2(f)(iii), carries the same 300 mm figure.

answers.answer: For a DN 80 underground water service running past (i.e. parallel to) another underground service, the minimum separation is 300 mm, because the pipe is greater than DN 65. Clause 5.3.3.6 states: "The separation between any underground water service pipe and any other service, other than consumer gas piping and electrical or communication service, shall be at least — (a) 100 mm for a water service pipe not greater than DN 65; or (b) 300 mm for a water service pipe greater than DN 65." So the 100 mm figure applies only to pipes DN 65 and smaller. Note that gas, electrical and communication services are excluded from 5.3.3.6 and have their own figures in 5.3.3.1–5.3.3.3 (e.g. 300 mm to a marked/protected consumer gas pipe or electrical cable for a water pipe > DN 65, 100 mm to a communication cable); drainage has its own rules in 5.3.3.4; non-drinking water in 5.3.3.5. If the alignment also crosses the other service, Clause 5.3.4 additionally requires crossing at not less than 45° with a vertical separation of not less than 100 mm, plus marker tape 1 m either side of the centre-line laid 150 mm above the service. answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.1:2021, Clause 5.5.4 'Under concrete slabs', item (a) requires a minimum distance of 75 mm between the top of the water service pipe and the underside of the slab or slab-stiffening beam. The same item also requires the pipe ends to be crimped or capped before the concrete is poured. (The clause appears as 5.5.4 in the 2021 edition; the same 75 mm figure appears as clause 5.4.4 in the superseded 2015 and 2018 editions, which are not the edition asked about.)

answers.answer: Table 5.18.2(A) of AS/NZS 3500.1:2021 gives a minimum thermal insulation thickness of 4 mm for a DN 20 pipe where the insulating material has a thermal conductivity of 0.03 W/m.K. The table lists pipe sizes 15, 18 and 20 in one group, with thicknesses of 9 mm, 6 mm and 4 mm respectively under the 0.03 W/m.K column, so DN 20 = 4 mm. This table is applied by Clause 5.18.2(b) (pipes outside buildings surrounded with waterproof thermal insulation) and Clause 5.18.5 (pipes in the areas listed in 5.18.4.1), and it is also the thickness referred to in Clause 5.18.3 for pipework across metal roofs. Note that the thicknesses were calculated per BS 5422 to just prevent freezing of water initially at 15 °C when exposed to −5 °C ambient for 8 h, and NOTE 1 to Clause 5.18.5 says additional thickness may be necessary where conditions are particularly severe over an extended time.

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.1:2021 Clause 7.2(a), a Type A system is defined as "All permanently open outlets and piping more than 150 mm above finished ground level, not subject to ponding or back-pressure and not involving injection systems. No backflow prevention required". So the outlets and piping must be installed more than 150 mm above finished ground level — i.e. 150 mm is the minimum height, and the threshold must be exceeded. Figure 7.2(A) on the same page annotates the Type A arrangement as "150 mm min. height above finished surface level and clear of surface ponding". Note the clause expresses the requirement as "more than 150 mm", not "not less than 150 mm"; systems at or below that level fall into the Type B/C categories (Clauses 7.2(b) and 7.2(c)) which require backflow prevention.
values: more than 150 mm above finished ground level (150 mm min.)

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.1:2021, Clause 8.4.4.1 ('General', part of Clause 8.4.4 Tank overflow), an overflow pipe from a cold water storage tank shall be 'not smaller than DN 40'. That is the minimum size; the clause adds that the overflow must also be 'capable of discharging the inflow rates given in Table 8.4.4.1 and the outflow rates specified in Figures 8.4.4.1(A), 8.4.4.1(B) and 8.4.4.1(C) or hydraulically calculated, taking into account the maximum head available in the main (but not less than 500 kPa), friction losses, elevation of the tank, size of the orifice and type of overflow outlet'. Figure 8.4.1 in the same section likewise labels the overflow pipe 'DN 40 min. (Clause 8.4.4)'. Note the related but separate requirement for a safe-tray overflow drain (Clause 8.8.3(a)), which must have an internal diameter greater than the tank overflow and not less than DN 50 in Australia (DN 40 in New Zealand) — that is a different pipe from the tank overflow itself.

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.1:2021, Clause 8.8.1(a), where a storage tank is external to the building (or located on an impervious floor graded to an outlet), no portion of the tank may be closer than 75 mm to a vertical line taken from the edge of the safe-tray. (A separate, smaller dimension of 25 mm applies to any attached auxiliary part.) The clause reads: "have no portion of the tank closer than 75 mm to a vertical line from the edge of the safe-tray and no portion of an attached auxiliary part closer than 25 mm to such vertical line". Note that Clause 8.8.1 also requires the tank to sit on durable supports not less than 12 mm thick, and the support must not come closer than 20 mm to the sides of the safe-tray — do not confuse that 20 mm support dimension with the 75 mm tank clearance asked about.

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.2:2021, Clause 3.5.1(b), where the presence of an obstacle prevents the drain from being laid at an even grade with the required cover, the drain is to pass beneath the obstacle at an even grade with a jump-up only at the point of connection. Alternatively, a minimum clearance of 25 mm shall be provided between the obstacle and the drain (or an inclined section may be installed adjacent to the obstacle as a graded jump-up with changes of direction not greater than 60°). Note this 25 mm obstacle-clearance figure is distinct from the 100 mm clearance required from underground obstructions under Clause 3.6.8 and the 100 mm clearance in easements under Clause 3.5.2(b).

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.2:2021, Clause 3.6.8 (Clearance from underground obstructions) requires drains to be installed with sufficient clearance to any underground obstruction to protect the drain from physical damage and to permit repairs, and states: "The clearance shall be at least 100 mm." So the minimum clearance is 100 mm. Clause 3.6.8 also notes: "See Clause 3.8 for drains in proximity to footings and foundations" (where, for example, 3.8.2(a) requires a minimum clearance of 25 mm between the top of the drain and the underside of a strip footing, and 3.8.2(b) an annular space of not less than 25 mm through footings or walls). Do not confuse the 100 mm obstruction clearance with Clause 3.5.1(b), which allows a minimum clearance of 25 mm between an obstacle and the drain where the presence of an obstacle prevents the drain being laid at an even grade with the required cover (that provision deals with grade/cover, not the general protection-from-damage clearance). Edition note: the library holds AS/NZS 3500.2:2021 (published); the 2025 edition (published 2025-04-17) is not held, so check the current edition for any change. Decision support only — not a substitute for a licensed practitioner's judgement.

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.2:2021 Clause 3.10.4, where a fixture discharge pipe is the same size as the unvented branch drain it connects to, the drain to the trap may have a maximum of two vertical jump-ups, each not exceeding 2 m in height, and they must be separated by not less than 300 mm of graded pipe. So: maximum height of each vertical jump-up = 2 m; minimum length of graded pipe between jump-ups = 300 mm (and no more than two jump-ups are permitted). answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.2:2021 the total length of the branch connections to fixtures when ground-floor fixtures are connected to unvented branch drains must not exceed 10 m. This is stated in the note to Figure 3.10.3 ('Typical connections of ground-floor fixtures to unvented branch drains'): 'NOTE Total length of branch connections to fixtures to not exceed 10 m.' The same 10 m limit is set by Clause 3.10.3: 'The total length of an unvented branch drain, including the length of the fixture discharge pipe, shall be not greater than the following: (a) 10 m from the vented drain to the weir of the trap …'; the sub-limits in (a)(i)–(iii) (2 m for WC pans with DN 80 discharge pipes, 1.5 m for basins and bidets with 'S' traps, 2.5 m for all other fixtures) apply only to the vertical drop between the crown of the trap and the invert of the branch drain, not to the total length. Clause 10.11.2 (p.163) confirms that the maximum length and size of any unvented graded pipe, branch or fixture discharge pipe shall be in accordance with Clause 3.10 and that the total length of an unvented branch pipe, including the fixture discharge pipe, shall be in accordance with Clause 3.10.3.

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.2:2021, Clause 3.19.2(b), drains from septic or sullage tanks to the common effluent drain must be laid at a grade of not less than 1% (1 in 100). answers.answer: Under Clause 4.6.5 of AS/NZS 3500.2:2021, where a disconnector gully is located inside a building, the vent branching from the riser pipe (or a fitting) must be a minimum nominal size of DN 50. Clause 4.6.5(b) states: "a DN 50 vent pipe, branching from the riser pipe or a fitting, extends at a grade of not less than 1.25 % and terminates with a grating at an external wall of the building". The same clause also requires the vent to terminate above the overflow level of the lowest internal fixture connected to the sealed disconnector gully, at least 75 mm above finished surface level, and (in areas likely to be inundated) in accordance with Clause 4.6.6.8; fixtures/appliances must not be connected to the vent pipe and air admittance valves must not be used to vent sealed disconnector gullies (Clauses 4.6.5(c) and (d)).

The same 1.25 % (1:80) minimum grade is stated generally for vents in Clause 6.9.2: "Vents shall be installed at a minimum grade of 1.25 % (1:80) so that any condensation or other liquids that form in or enter the vent will drain to the sanitary plumbing and sanitary drainage system." Clause 4.6.5(c)–(d) add that no fixtures or appliances may be connected to the vent pipe and air admittance valves must not be used to vent sealed disconnector gullies (where it is not practicable to extend the vent to an external wall, it may terminate in the atmosphere external to the building in accordance with Clause 6.9.4).

answers.answer: Clause 4.6.6.6 of AS/NZS 3500.2:2021 requires a minimum height of 150 mm between the top of the overflow gully riser and the lowest fixture connected to the drain: "A minimum height of 150 mm shall be maintained between the top of the overflow gully riser and the lowest fixture connected to the drain. This height shall be measured vertically from the overflow level of the gully riser or from the invert level of the overflow pipe to the point given in Table 4.6.6.6." The height is therefore measured vertically from the overflow level of the gully riser (or the invert of the overflow pipe) to the fixture measuring point listed in Table 4.6.6.6 — e.g. top surface level of the water seal for a soil fixture with an integral trap, top surface level of the grate for a floor waste gully or shower, overflow rim for a soil fixture in an outbuilding/room graded to an external doorway, and top surface level of the fixture outlet for other fixtures (including greywater diversion devices). Note this 150 mm is distinct from the separate 75 mm minimum required by Clause 4.6.6.7 between the top of the riser (or invert of the overflow pipe) and the finished surface level. If the 150 mm cannot be achieved, Clause 4.5.2(a) requires a reflux valve. answers.answer: Where a floor waste gully has submerged inlets, the minimum height of the gully riser is 100 mm, measured from the top of the water seal to the floor surface level. Clause 4.6.7.7 states "The height of the gully riser shall be measured from the top of the water seal to the floor surface level and conform to the following:" and then, at 4.6.7.7(b), "For floor waste gullies with submerged inlets, the minimum height shall be 100 mm." (NOTE to that clause: the maximum height may be extended to 1 m when receiving the discharges from plant rooms located above ground floor level.) This is separate from the 600 mm maximum in 4.6.7.7(a)(ii) and from Table 4.6.7.7, which sets minimum heights for gullies with waste connections to the riser (200/150 mm for 88° entry, 150/100 mm for 45° entry). answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.2:2021 Clause 5.5.2 (Excavated material), excavated material from the trench may be used for final backfill provided it is free from rock, hard matter and organic material and is broken up so that it does not contain soil lumps larger than 75 mm. A related but separate requirement sits in Clause 5.4.4 for bedding/backfill immediately around the pipe: backfill shall also be free from builder's waste, bricks, concrete pieces, rocks or hard matter larger than 25 mm.

answers.answer: The 25 mm minimum you are asking about is stated in Clause 6.5.1 (General), not in Clause 6.5.2. AS/NZS 3500.2:2021, Clause 6.5.1 (p.85) reads: "Under normal operating conditions, fixture traps shall retain a water seal of not less than 25 mm." Clause 6.5.2 ("Water seal", p.85) deals with a different case — traps in a pressurized chamber — and requires: "Traps that are installed in a pressurized chamber shall retain a water seal of not less than 70 mm when the maximum pressure within the chamber is applied." The same 25 mm figure is repeated for post-testing residual seals in Clause 15.1 (p.189): "the residual water seal in the trap of the fixture concerned or in any other trap connected to the same system shall, under normal operating conditions, retain a water seal of not less than 25 mm." Note the library holds the 2021 edition only; the 2025 edition of AS/NZS 3500.2 (published 2025-04-17) is one edition ahead and is not in the knowledge base, so check it for any change. answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.2:2021, Clause 6.6.2.4.2 ("New installations"), where a junction is used to make the connection of a DN 100 branch pipe to another DN 100 pipe, the entry level of the branch pipe shall be elevated at an incline of not less than 15° above the horizontal (this is a sanitary plumbing/discharge pipe requirement — the parallel drain requirement in Clause 4.9.1.2 is the same figure). The standard explains that positioning the junction a minimum of 15° above horizontal removes the probability of the partial backwash of a discharge into the branch causing stranding that can lead to blockages in the pipe. Note the on-grade allowance in Clause 6.6.2.4.3 applies only to other installations — repairs or extensions to existing installations, where WC pans are not connected upstream, or where the main and branch pipes are not DN 100 — so it does not apply to this new DN 100 to DN 100 connection.

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.2:2021 the minimum size of a branch vent is set by the size of the branch DISCHARGE pipe it serves, not by the size of the group vent it connects to; the library contains no rule that sizes a branch vent from the DN of the group vent. Clause 8.5.2.1 states: 'The size of any branch vent shall be in accordance with Table 8.5.2.1', and Table 8.5.2.1 (Minimum size of branch vents) reads: branch discharge pipe DN 40 / 50 / 65 → branch vent DN 32 / 40 / 40; branch discharge pipe DN 80 / 100 / 150 → branch vent DN 50 / 50 / 80. So a branch vent serving a DN 40 branch discharge pipe is minimum DN 32 (which is what a DN 40 group vent — i.e. a group vent sized under Table 8.5.7.3 for a DN 50 common discharge pipe — would normally be met by). Clause 8.5.2.3 adds that where the branch discharge pipe varies in size along its length, 'the corresponding sections of a branch vent shall be sized separately in accordance with Table 8.5.2.1' and 'Any enlargement in size in the branch vent shall occur prior to the junction with the trap vent or group vent as shown in Figure 8.5.2.3' — that figure is an illustrative example showing a DN 40 group vent with a DN 40 branch vent increased to DN 50 at the junction, and is not the sizing rule. Note: the library holds the 2021 edition of AS/NZS 3500.2 (published, not superseded in the library); NCC 2025 calls up the 2025 edition, which is not held here. Jurisdiction: national (AS/NZS).

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.2:2021, Clause 8.5.7.5.4, a basin or bidet connected to a group-vented branch shall have a DN 40 trap and fixture discharge pipe not greater than 2.5 m in length, with a maximum vertical drop of 1.5 m. The maximum number of bends in a fixture discharge pipe shall be in accordance with Clause 9.5.4." The associated Figure 8.5.7.5.4 confirms "Vertical drop not to exceed 1.5 m" and "Total length 2.5 m max. DN 40". This ties in with Clause 8.5.7.5.2, which states "Group-vented branches shall be installed on a grade with a maximum vertical drop of 1.5 m." Note: the value asked about (the 1.5 m vertical drop limit) is the drop of the fixture discharge pipe/group-vented branch, not the fixture discharge pipe length; the length limit is 2.5 m.

answers.answer: The vent may be reduced to DN 50. AS/NZS 3500.2:2021 states: "Stacks that extend not more than three floor levels with a maximum loading of 30 fixture units may have the vent reduced to DN 50." This is the general venting rule (Clause 9.6 General — the sentence sits under the 9.6.1 General heading, immediately before 9.6.2 Cross-vents), and it qualifies the general requirement that "The stack shall continue to the vent cowl undiminished in size." A parallel provision appears for DN 50 vertical stack sections under Clause 9.8.9 (three waste fixtures — basins, showers or kitchen sinks — may connect to a DN 50 vertical stack section not more than three floor levels with a maximum loading of 30 fixture units), and for graded top sections under 9.8.4(c), where the graded section or vent shall not be smaller than DN 50. Edition used: AS/NZS 3500.2:2021 (published; not superseded in the library). Note: NCC 2025 calls up AS/NZS 3500.2 in its 2025 edition, which the library does not hold — the figure quoted is from the 2021 edition.

answers.answer: In a domestic or residential building, a DN 100 stack serving the first floor above ground level (i.e. one floor in height) with the top section graded (nominally horizontal), where fixtures discharge without vents on the fixture discharge pipes, may receive a maximum stack loading of 90 fixture units. Clause 9.8.5(b) states: 'The stack loading shall not exceed 90 fixture units.' The other conditions of Clause 9.8.5 also apply (individual fixture discharge pipes; connection to the graded section not less than 450 mm from the lower vertical section of the stack; no branches on the vertical sections within 600 mm below the lower bend forming part of the offset). Note the distinction from Clause 9.8.4 (p.145), where a DN 100 stack serving not more than three floor levels with the top section graded is limited to 30 fixture units.

answers.answer: Under Clause 16.10.4 of AS/NZS 3500.2:2021, the second stage lift pipe must be installed with a vacuum reforming pocket when it is greater than 900 mm. answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.2:2021, Clause 16.15.2 requires an initial vacuum test pressure of −55 ± 5 kPa applied to the section being tested. The text reads: "An initial vacuum test pressure of −55 ± 5 kPa shall be applied to the section being tested. When −55 ± 5 kPa has been reached, the vacuum pump and supply valve shall be shut off. The vacuum shall be allowed to stabilize for a minimum of 3 min while checking for leaks." The test then continues per Clause 16.15.3 by allowing the vacuum to fall to −50 kPa, with no drop greater than −1 kPa over the minimum test duration in Table 16.15.3. Note: this −55 ± 5 kPa figure applies to the Section 16 vacuum drainage system test; the general Section 15.4 vacuum test on sanitary plumbing/drainage uses approximately 15 kPa, so the two must not be confused.

answers.answer: For a vacuum drainage system, Clause 16.15.2 of AS/NZS 3500.2:2021 requires: "An initial vacuum test pressure of −55 ± 5 kPa shall be applied to the section being tested. When −55 ± 5 kPa has been reached, the vacuum pump and supply valve shall be shut off. The vacuum shall be allowed to stabilize for a minimum of 3 min while checking for leaks." (p.207). So the initial test pressure is −55 ± 5 kPa (i.e. 55 kPa below atmospheric, ± 5 kPa), and the vacuum must be allowed to stabilize for a minimum of 3 min while checking for leaks. Clause 16.15.1 (p.207) also requires all vacuum sanitary plumbing and drainage inlets, outlets and access openings to be capped and sealed before the test. After stabilization, Clause 16.15.2 (p.208) requires the test to commence by allowing the vacuum to fall to −50 kPa and then recording the time and drop in vacuum over the minimum test duration in Table 16.15.3, with a maximum permitted vacuum drop of −1 kPa. Note: this is distinct from the general vacuum test in Clause 15.4.2 for sanitary plumbing and drainage (Section 15), which uses an initial vacuum of approximately 15 kPa falling to 10 kPa over the Table 15.3.2 durations — that clause is not the vacuum drainage system test you asked about. answers.answer: Clause 2.13.1 of AS/NZS 3500.3:2021 requires natural sand used as filter material for subsoil drains to be well-graded and to have less than 5% passing a 75 μm sieve — i.e. the fines content must be below 5%, so 5% is the ceiling, not a permitted quantity. The full requirement reads: filter materials of natural clean washed sands and gravels and screened crushed rock shall be '(a) well-graded, with a mix of different sizes of sand particles and permeability with — (i) natural sand, less than 5 % passing a 75 μm sieve; and (ii) screened crushed rock, sizes 3 mm to 20 mm'. The clause also requires the material to be sufficiently coarse not to wash into the subsoil drain or through geotextile pores, and to be chemically stable and inert.

answers.answer:
The excerpts give two different figures depending on the part of the roof drainage system being sized, and the general minimum clause itself (Clause 3.5.3 Vertical downpipes, p.35) is named in the excerpt but its text was not supplied.

(a) Eaves gutter systems — Table 3.5.2 (Required size of vertical downpipe) is a stepped table whose smallest entry is 65 mm circular and 65 mm × 50 mm rectangular. The table's vertical downpipe column begins: 65 / 75 / 75 / 80 / 80 / 85 / 90 / 90 / 100 … (circular) against 65 × 50 / 65 × 50 / 75 × 50 / 75 × 50 / 100 × 50 … (rectangle or square). So for the smallest eaves gutter listed (effective cross-sectional area 3 500 mm² at 1:500 and steeper, 4 700 mm² flatter than 1:500), the smallest downpipe is 65 mm diameter or 65 mm × 50 mm.

(b) Box gutter / rainhead / sump downpipes — Clause 3.7.8 sets a floor value in words: "Downpipes shall be at least 90 mm in diameter or 100 mm × 50 mm rectangular downpipe, be fitted vertically to the base of a rainhead or sump …". This is the minimum permissible for downpipes from rainheads and sumps, and it is larger than the smallest eaves-gutter table entry.

Because the supplied text of Clause 3.5.3 (Vertical downpipes) is blank, whether it imposes an overall minimum that overrides the 65 mm table entry cannot be confirmed from these excerpts — check Clause 3.5.3 on p.35 of the source.
values: at least 90 mm diameter (Clause 3.7.8, rainhead/sump downpipes)

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.3:2021, Clause 6.3.3(a) sets the minimum diameter for a site stormwater drain serving a single dwelling on an urban allotment of less than 1 000 m² at DN 90. That figure applies to the drain upstream of any pit; once the drain is downstream of a stormwater or inlet pit, Clause 6.3.3(b) requires a larger minimum diameter: the greatest of the diameter of the largest pipe entering the pit, DN 150 (Australia) or DN 100 (New Zealand). The informative worked example in Appendix J confirms this split for a house on an urban allotment of not more than 1 000 m²: 'Between a downpipe outlet and a stormwater or inlet pit, DN 90' and 'Between the stormwater, pits A and B, DN 150'. For the described allotment (Australia), the minimum pipe diameter is therefore DN 90 between the downpipe outlet and the first pit, and DN 150 downstream of a pit.

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.3:2021, Clause 7.5.3 ("Falls across pits") distinguishes pits with and without a sump. For a sump pit in a site stormwater drain, the floor must be flat, with a fall of at least 20 mm between the inverts of the inlet and outlet pipes: "Sump pits shall have a flat floor but a fall of at least 20 mm between pipe inverts, as shown in Figure 7.5.3 (b)." (By contrast, a pit without a sump must have the floor graded to fall at least 20 mm between the pipe inverts.) The same 20 mm minimum fall is confirmed in the informative worked examples, where Column 13 gives "for each pit the minimum fall from the upstream to the downstream invert levels of 20 mm, see Clause 7.5.3", and in Clause J.2.3(b). The clause sits within Section 7 ("Surface water and subsoil drainage systems — Ancillaries"), and Clause 7.5.1.2 also requires inlet pits, where used, to allow collection and ingress of stormwater to a site stormwater drain and to operate as an inlet pit.

answers.answer: Clause 7.5.5.6 'Upper walls of stormwater pits' requires the upper walls to be either (a) vertical, or (b) tapered upwards to the access shaft from a point not less than — (i) 1 500 mm above the invert of the outlet pipe; and (ii) 100 mm above the top of the highest inlet pipe. So the taper must start not less than 1 500 mm above the outlet invert (and not less than 100 mm above the top of the highest inlet pipe). The same clause states: 'The diameter of the access shaft shall be not less than 600 mm, and its length not greater than 350 mm' — i.e. minimum access shaft diameter 600 mm, maximum access shaft length 350 mm. Edition used: AS/NZS 3500.3:2021 (published, the edition held in the library and the edition named in the question). answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.3:2021, Clause 7.8(a), the bend at the base of a jump-up in a site stormwater drain must be supported on a concrete footing of a thickness not less than 100 mm, extending upwards not less than 100 mm. Clause 7.8 reads: "Jump-ups in site stormwater drains shall be constructed in accordance with the following: (a) The bend at the base of the jump-up shall be supported on a concrete footing of a thickness not less than 100 mm and extending upwards not less than 100 mm." Note: do not confuse this with Clause 7.9 anchor blocks (required where the gradient exceeds 1:5), which must be not less than 150 mm thick and extend not less than 150 mm above the drain and 150 mm below the trench foundation — that is a different requirement for a different situation.

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.3:2021 Clause 7.9, where the gradient of a site stormwater drain exceeds 1:5, anchor blocks shall be installed at the bend or junction at the top and bottom of the inclined drain (Figure 7.9) and at intervals not exceeding 3 m. answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.3:2021, Clause 7.10.2(c) requires that where a below-ground on-site stormwater detention (OSD) tank exceeds 1.2 m in depth, a ladder complying with Clause 7.5.5.4 must be installed: "Where the depth of the tank exceeds 1.2 m, a ladder in accordance with Clause 7.5.5.4 shall be installed." The same file also sets the inspection/access opening size (Clause 7.10.2(b)(ii), p.101): an opening at least 600 mm × 600 mm (or 600 mm diameter) for storages up to 800 mm deep, and 600 mm × 900 mm for deeper storages, located above the outlet, with no impediments to removal of debris and possible to inspect without residents or owners having to remove heavy access covers. Note that the same 1.2 m/ladder rule is repeated for pumped-system wet wells in Clause 8.3.5, but that clause applies to wet wells, not storage tanks.

answers.answer: For an air test of downpipes within buildings, AS/NZS 3500.3:2021 Clause 9.3.1(b) requires an air test at a pressure of not less than 30 kPa for a period of not less than 3 min. Clause 9.3 gives the two alternatives for downpipes within buildings: '(a) a water test at a pressure of a head of water equal to the lesser of 10 m or the length of the downpipe for a period of not less than 10 min; or (b) an air test at a pressure of not less than 30 kPa for a period of not less than 3 min. NOTE 1 kPa = 100 mm head of water.' Note: the 3 min hold is the test criterion for downpipes within buildings; the additional pressure-drop timing in Clause 9.3.2(b)/9.4.2 (30 kPa held 3 min, then time for drop from 25 kPa to 20 kPa to exceed 90 s or 180 s) applies to site stormwater drains, drains within and under buildings, and main internal drains — not to downpipes within buildings. Likewise the 30 min period in Appendix N (informative) relates to siphonic systems and is informative only. Decision support only — not a substitute for a licensed practitioner's judgement.

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.3:2021, Clause 9.4 (Procedure) states: "The head of water on any section of drain shall not exceed 3 m." So the maximum head of water that shall not be exceeded when water-testing a section of below-ground drain is 3 m. This is consistent with Clause 9.3.2(a), which sets the water test pressure for site stormwater drains, drains within and under buildings, and main internal drains as a pressure "within the range 1.5 m to 3.0 m head of water", maintained for not less than 10 min (FRC, precast concrete (steel reinforced) and vitrified clay (ceramic) products) or 5 min (all other products), with leakage not exceeding Table 9.3.2(A). (The 3 m cap is the test-head limit; it is not the downpipe test head in Clause 9.3.1(a), which is the lesser of 10 m or the length of the downpipe.) Edition used: AS/NZS 3500.3:2021, published and not superseded in the library; note that NCC 2025 calls up the 2025 edition of AS/NZS 3500.3, which is not held in this library.

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.1:2018 Clause 5.2.10, water service pipes must be installed with sufficient clearance to any underground obstruction to protect the service from physical damage and to permit repairs, with the minimum clearance being 100 mm for a water service not exceeding DN 65 and 300 mm for a water service exceeding DN 65. A DN 50 pipe does not exceed DN 65, so the minimum clearance is 100 mm. Note: the 2018 edition held in the library is marked superseded (the library's current edition for this Part is AS/NZS 3500.1:2021); the same 100 mm / 300 mm rule appears in the 2003 edition at Clause 5.3.10.

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.1:2018, Clause 5.4.4(c) requires any pipework penetrating a slab on ground to be at right angles to the slab surface and lagged for the full depth of the slab penetration with either (i) an impermeable flexible material of not less than 6 mm thickness, or (ii) an impermeable plastics sleeve or conduit providing equivalent protection. So the minimum thickness of impermeable flexible lagging is 6 mm. Note: the 2018 edition held in the library is marked superseded; the equivalent provision in the published AS/NZS 3500.1:2021 is Clause 5.5.4(c) (p.48) and carries the same 6 mm figure.

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.1:2018, Clause 5.9 'Depth of cover' requires that where water services are installed below ground, the minimum cover shall be as specified in Table 5.9, measured from the proposed finished surface levels. answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.1:2018, Clause 5.17.4.2 (Pipes in unheated roof spaces), pipes in unheated roof spaces shall be located not less than 100 mm away from the roof covering and external walls. answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.1:2018 Clause 8.7 (p.68), a sludge valve must be fitted where the tank capacity exceeds 500 L, and its minimum size is DN 40 — provided the valve is also not less than half the outlet pipe size. Clause 8.7 reads: "A sludge valve shall be fitted where the capacity of the tank exceeds 500 L. The minimum size of the valve shall be not less than half the outlet pipe size nor less than DN 40." So the floor value is DN 40, and the actual minimum is the greater of DN 40 and half the outlet pipe size. Note the edition: this file's edition_status is superseded — AS/NZS 3500.1:2018 has been replaced (the library holds AS/NZS 3500.1:2021 as the current edition), and NCC 2025 calls up the 2025 edition, which the library does not hold.

answers.answer: AS/NZS 3500.1:2018, Clause 18.3.1 (Hydrostatic test) requires that water services not show any leakage when subjected to a hydrostatic pressure of 1500 kPa for a period of not less than 30 min. The clause adds that the test shall be performed on installed piping prior to burial or concealment, and that for pipe systems with elastomeric seals the piping shall be backfilled leaving the joints exposed until completion of the test. Note: the library's copy of this edition is marked superseded (the current edition held is AS/NZS 3500.1:2021), but the clause answers the question as asked for the 2018 edition.

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.2:2018, copper alloy bends and junctions used at the base of stacks greater than 9 m in height must be cast or hot-pressed. The library text reads: "Copper alloy bends and junctions used at the base of stacks greater than 9 m in height shall be cast or hot-pressed" (Clause 2.4.2(d), p.17). Note the related provision for shorter stacks: fabricated copper bends and junctions at the base of stacks up to 9 m in height must be formed of Type B or heavier gauge copper (Clause 2.4.3(b), p.17). Edition caveat: the file used is AS/NZS 3500.2:2018, which is marked edition_status: superseded in the library; the library's latest held edition is AS/NZS 3500.2:2021, and NCC 2025 calls up the 2025 edition (published 2025-04-17, not held). The 2018 wording is quoted only because the question names that edition.

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.2:2018 Clause 4.6.6.6 ('Height of overflow point below lowest fixture'), a minimum height of 150 mm shall be maintained between the top of the overflow gully riser and the lowest fixture connected to the drain. The height is measured vertically from the overflow level of the gully riser, or from the invert level of the overflow pipe, to the appropriate point on the fixture given in Table 4.6.6.6 (e.g. top surface level of the water seal for a soil fixture with integral trap; top surface level of the grate for a floor waste gully or shower). Note: this file is marked edition_status: superseded, so the 150 mm figure is quoted from the superseded 2018 edition as asked, not as the current requirement.

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.2:2018 the maximum length of an untrapped waste pipe connected to the riser of a floor waste gully is 1.2 m. Table 4.6.7.2 'Discharge to floor waste gullies' gives 1.2 m in the 'Fixture untrapped' / 'Connected to riser of floor waste gully' column for every fixture listed as permitted untrapped (bain-marie/sterilizer, bar sink, bath/shower, bidet, cleaners' sink, clothes-washing machine, laundry and ablution trough, refrigerated cabinet, shower, etc.); tundishes are the exception at 10.0 m. Basins and drinking fountains are 'Not permitted' as untrapped connections, and for a submerged-inlet floor waste gully untrapped fixtures are 'Not allowed' (only trapped fixtures, 2.5 m). Clause 4.6.7.3 reinforces this: each fixture or fixture pair connected to a floor waste gully 'shall be connected by a separate waste pipe at a grade of not less than 2.5% and with a length not exceeding that specified in Table 4.6.7.2'. Appendix B repeats 1.2 m for untrapped DN 40/DN 50 wastes to a floor waste gully. Note: the held file is marked edition_status: superseded (AS/NZS 3500.2 has since been revised; check the current edition for the same table).

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.2:2018, Clause 6.8.1(b) governs stacks of two floor levels or less: no connection shall be made closer than 500 mm downstream or upstream of the base of the stack. So the minimum distance upstream from the base of the stack at which a discharge pipe may connect is 500 mm. In addition, Clause 6.8.1(b)(ii) requires that no discharge pipe connecting a fixture upstream of a junction that connects a stack to a drain or graded pipe shall be within 500 mm of the base of the stack. Note this edition is superseded (the library holds AS/NZS 3500.2:2021 as the current edition, and NCC 2025 calls up the 2025 edition).

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.2:2018, Clause 9.2.5 ('Number of floor levels'), the floor levels counted against Tables 9.7.1(A)/9.7.1(B)/9.7.2(A)/9.7.2(B) are counted from the point where the stack connects to the drain or graded pipe up to the highest floor level on which a fixture is connected. Where the distance between the invert of the drain or graded pipe and the lowest floor level EXCEEDS 2.4 m, that lowest floor is counted as an additional floor level. So the trigger is a distance greater than 2.4 m (i.e. 2.4 m or less does not add a floor level). Figure 9.2.5 gives worked examples of the floor-level count, annotated 'If > 2.4 m (See Clause 9.2.5)'. Note on edition: the excerpt is marked edition_status: superseded — AS/NZS 3500.2:2018 has since been superseded (the library also holds AS/NZS 3500.2:2021, and NCC 2025 calls up the 2025 edition); confirm the current edition's figure before relying on this for a current design.

answers.answer: For a DN 100 stack with a graded offset installed between the base of the stack and the highest connection, AS/NZS 3500.2:2018 Clause 9.9.5 (Graded offsets) requires the minimum distance between the centre-lines of the vertical sections of the stack to be 2 m. Clause 9.9.5 also limits the arrangement to one graded offset per stack, a stack height not exceeding 10 consecutive floor levels, and fixture connection in accordance with Clause 8.6.2. Note the distinction: the 1 m figure in Clause 9.8.7.1(b) applies to a waste stack up to DN 100 with a graded offset between the highest and lowest connections, not to the DN 100 stack offset between base and highest connection covered by 9.9.5. The excerpt text of 9.9.5 is OCR-garbled in places (the words 'shall be 2 m' sit out of order relative to sub-clause (c)); check p.145 of the original for critical use. This edition is recorded as superseded. Decision support only — not a substitute for a licensed practitioner's judgement.
values: 2 m minimum distance between centre-lines of vertical sections (Clause 9.9.5(c))
One graded offset only per stack (9.9.5(a))
Stack height not exceeding 10 consecutive floor levels (9.9.5(b))
Contrast: 1 m for DN 100 waste stack graded offset between highest and lowest connections (9.8.7.1(b))

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.2:2018, Clause 15.1, sanitary fixtures are tested by subjecting them to normal use, and after each test the residual water seal in the trap of the fixture concerned (or in any other trap connected to the same system) must, under normal operating conditions, retain a water seal of not less than 25 mm. Where a 25 mm seal cannot be retained, the system must be inspected to determine the cause, modified/repaired, and the fixture retested. Note: the 2018 edition held in the library is marked superseded (by AS/NZS 3500.2:2021); the 2021 edition retains the same 25 mm requirement in its Clause 15.1 (p.189).

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.2:2018, where hydrostatic (water) testing is used on a sanitary drainage installation, the pipe shall be filled with water to a height of not less than 1 m above the soffit level at the highest point of the section being tested (Clause 15.2(a), p.177). Two related limits in the same clause: for sanitary plumbing the water is taken to the spill level of the highest fixture or the flood level of the lowest sanitary fixture, whichever is higher (15.2(b)); and in either case the head must not exceed 3 m at the lowest point of the test section (15.2(c)). The pressure must then be maintained without leakage for at least 15 min. Note: the file's edition_status is 'superseded' — this is the 2018 edition as asked; NCC 2025 calls up the 2025 editions of AS/NZS 3500 Parts 1–4, and the library holds the 2021 edition as its latest (2025 edition not held), so the 2018 figure may not reflect the current edition.
values: 1 m (not less than) above the soffit level at the highest point of the section being tested

answers.answer: Clause 4.7.2.3 of AS/NZS 3500.3:2018 states: "The laps for eaves gutters shall be not less than 25 mm." answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.3:2018, Clause 5.4.10.2 (On-grade pits), the blockage factor to be used for on-grade pits is 0.8 — reducing inlet capacities to 80% of the values given by design aids. The clause states that inlet capacities of on-grade pits vary considerably with the shape and size of pit and that blockage factors are variable, but that "a value of 0.8 (reducing capacities to 80% of values given by design aids) shall be used for on-grade pits." Note on edition: the 2018 edition in the knowledge base is marked superseded; the same wording appears in AS/NZS 3500.3:2021, Clause 5.4.10.2 (p.72), which is the published edition held. Also note this is distinct from the sag-pit inlet equation 5.4.10.1, where the blockage factor bf has a common value of 0.5 (NOTE only, not a mandatory value).

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.3:2018, Clause 5.4.11.2 (Design procedure) step (d) caps the full-pipe velocity for site stormwater pipe drains at 2.0 m/s: "If the pipe hydraulic capacity is less than the design flow, assume a new DN for the pipe drain and repeat Step (c) until the hydraulic capacity exceeds the design flow. The full-pipe velocity shall not exceed 2.0 m/s." A NOTE to the same clause adds a lower, non-mandatory target for outlet pipes: "To reduce the possibility of overflow from stormwater pits due to increased energy losses, the full-pipe velocity in the outlet pipe should not exceed 1.5 m/s." The 1.5 m/s figure also appears in the worked example in Appendix K (Clause K3.3.2, p.164) as a design check ("If, for other than steep gradients, the full pipe velocity exceeds 1.5 m/s select a larger pipe diameter"), but the binding limit in Clause 5.4.11.2 is 2.0 m/s. Edition note: the library copy of AS/NZS 3500.3:2018 is marked superseded (the library also holds the later AS/NZS 3500.3:2021), so confirm against the current edition if the project requires it.

answers.answer: Under AS/NZS 3500.3:2018, Clause 7.5.3(b) requires that pits without a sump have the floor graded to fall at least 20 mm between the inverts of the inlet and outlet pipes. AS/NZS 3500.3:2018 requires tank floors in below-ground on-site stormwater detention (OSD) systems with open storage zones to be graded at a minimum slope of 1:140 towards the outlet, to minimize ponding and depositing of debris — clause 7.10.2(b)(i), p.92. AS/NZS 3500.3:2021, Clause 7.10.2(b)(iv) requires the sump in a discharge control pit within the storage to be set a minimum of 1.5 times the diameter of the orifice of the outlet below the centre of the orifice — not 4 times. answers.answer: No — the premise that Clause 4.3.2 "requires 2.4000000000000004" is wrong: that figure appears nowhere in the clause or in Table 4.3.2 (it looks like a floating-point artefact, not a library value). For a **copper** box gutter with **base metal thickness 0.80 mm**, in the Table 4.3.2 column "Maximum length between expansion joints, m — One end fixed and one end free to move", the library gives **15 m**. Clause 4.3.2(a) states: "For box gutters and support systems, the maximum lengths between expansion joints and minimum expansion space shall be as given in Table 4.3.2 … The maximum lengths between expansion joints in Table 4.3.2 shall apply from the fixed point to the free end(s)." The copper row of Table 4.3.2 reads: base metal thickness 0.60 / 0.80 / 1.00 mm → 9 / 15 / 26 m (one end fixed, one end free), 18 / 30 / 52 m (both ends free), minimum expansion space 50 mm. So the 0.80 mm copper value is **15 m**, not 2.4 m.

Quoting the held 2021 edition (published): Clause 7.5.3 'Falls across pits' (p.94) — 'Pits without a sump, as shown in Figure 7.5.3 (a), shall have the floor graded to fall at least 20 mm between the inverts of the inlet and outlet pipes. So for a sump pit in a site stormwater drain: fall of at least 20 mm between the pipe inverts, and the sump pit floor is to be flat (not graded) — the 20 mm fall being between pipe inverts, not in the floor. The same wording appears in the superseded 2018 edition, Clause 7.5.3 (p.85). Decision support only — not a substitute for a licensed practitioner's judgement.

answers.answer: AS/NZS 3500.3:2025 is not in the knowledge base, so no 2025 figure can be given. The latest edition held is AS/NZS 3500.3:2021 (published, not superseded). Under that edition, Clause 8.3.6 'Combined effective storage' requires the minimum wet well storage between the high and low working levels, expressed in cubic metres, to be '1 % of the catchment area in m2 and not less than 3 m3'. The same clause requires the combined effective storage (volume able to be pumped in 30 min plus wet well storage) to be not less than the run-off from the storm of 10 % AEP (10 years ARI) and duration of 120 min, with maximum pump capacity as detailed in Clause 8.4(a). Note the library's 2003, 2015 and 2018 editions are superseded and state the same 1 % of catchment area / not less than 3 m3 minimum.

answers.answer: AS/NZS 3500.3:2025 is not held in the knowledge base (the library's latest published edition of Part 3 is 2021), so Clause 3.7.8 of the 2025 edition cannot be quoted and no 2025 figure can be given. What the held edition says, labelled with its year: AS/NZS 3500.3:2021, Clause 3.7.8 'Downpipes' (p.50) states — 'Downpipes shall be at least 90 mm in diameter or 100 mm × 50 mm rectangular downpipe, be fitted vertically to the base of a rainhead or sump, and discharge to — (a) a rainhead or sump of a lower gutter; or (b) a surface water drainage system with the capacity to convey run-off from a storm event in accordance with Table 3.3.4.' In that edition (published, not superseded) the minimum is therefore 90 mm diameter, or 100 mm × 50 mm for a rectangular downpipe.
